title: Pastry with Bean or Lotus Seed Paste

content.title: About
content.content: Pastry with bean or lotus seed paste filling is a traditional East Asian dessert made from baked dough with a sweet, smooth interior. The bean paste (often red bean) or lotus seed paste provides a delicate sweetness and aromatic flavor characteristic of many Asian cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bean‑paste pastries are popular in China, Japan and Korea, where they are known as “mochi” or “dango”.
Lotus seed paste is made by cooking lotus seeds until soft and grinding them into a fine, sweet mass.
The dough is typically prepared from wheat flour, eggs, sugar and butter, giving the pastry a light, airy texture.
These pastries are traditionally served during tea ceremonies and festive meals.
In some regions the filling is flavored with spices such as ginger or cinnamon for extra aroma.

items.title: Rich plant protein source
items.content: Both beans and lotus seeds contain notable amounts of protein, important for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: High dietary fiber
items.content: The pastes are rich in fiber, which supports healthy digestion and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamin content
items.content: Beans provide B1, B6 and folate, vitamins involved in energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Lotus seeds and beans supply iron, magnesium and potassium, beneficial for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phenolic compounds in bean paste act as antioxidants, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Bean allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The filling is often sweetened, so people with diabetes or those watching their weight should limit consumption.

items.title: Gluten in the dough
items.content: Traditional pastry dough contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Baked pastries with butter and sugar can be calorie‑dense; moderation is key for energy balance.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pastry warm or at room temperature as a standalone dessert or alongside tea. It is often cut into bite‑size pieces and garnished with edible flowers or nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pastries in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. They can be refrigerated for up to a week, or frozen for longer storage, wrapped tightly in plastic film.
